The Canadian read

Canada is a firm-led market, and that changes the first year.

The Canadian legal AI market is not a smaller copy of the US one. Adoption here has been led by the firms. Every Canadian customer Legora has named publicly is a law firm and not a corporate legal department: McMillan and Stewart McKelvey directly, McCarthy Tétrault and Fasken through the Walter acquisition, with Fasken going firm-wide in July 2026. That is a national footprint spanning Bay Street, Montréal, and Atlantic Canada, built firm-side first.

What that means commercially

Firm-wide deployment is a partnership sale, not a seat sale. The buying centre is a managing partner, an innovation or knowledge lead, a CIO, and a risk committee, and the deal is decided in rooms the vendor is not invited to. That is the same shape as the enterprise platform deals I have run for a decade.

Where the second wave comes from

Firms are the distribution channel into their own clients. Every firm-wide deployment creates a warm path to the general counsel on the other side of the engagement. The in-house segment in Canada is a follow-on motion earned through firm reference, not a parallel one opened cold.

The gate is not the demo

Canadian firms and banks decide on privilege, data residency, retention, and audit trail. In my experience the product wins the room and the security review decides the outcome. Teams that treat the review as a late-stage formality lose quarters to it.

The competitive frame

The primary competitor opened in Toronto in October 2025, roughly six months ahead of Legora. In a concentrated market with a small number of decisive logos, that makes this a displacement and catch-up mandate rather than a greenfield one. Win rate against one named competitor matters more than pipeline volume, and reference density inside a practice area compounds faster than any outbound programme.

Demos sell. Audits ship.

The mandate

Four things a revenue leader actually owns.

Read against the posting, this role is a hands-on revenue leadership job: carry the team’s number, coach daily, sponsor the largest deals personally, and build the playbook out of live cycles rather than in advance. Here is what I bring to each.

01 · Build and keep the team

I built a ten-person enterprise account executive team across six North American offices, delivering roughly $12M annually and more than 30% of total vertical revenue, and carried three and a half years of first-line people management before that with full P&L ownership at Enterprise Rent-A-Car. Development is the retention strategy, not a perk attached to one.

02 · Sponsor the complex deals

I take a named role as executive sponsor and door opener while the rep keeps the opportunity, the forecast, and the relationship. Present in the deal, never the owner of it. That is how you coach a seven-figure cycle without quietly taking it over.

03 · Navigate the regulated buying centre

Financial services, healthcare and life sciences, and national retail, including privacy and governance frameworks at Loblaw across more than twenty lines of business and its financial services and banking operations. Professional services firms run the same review, with privilege added on top.

04 · Run the operating rigor

Forecast accuracy, pipeline hygiene, conversion and cycle-length analysis, and territory decisions made on evidence. I built dashboards, pipeline alerting, and Slack-integrated reporting across six offices without a revenue operations function to lean on.

Selling the aOS

An operating system is a different sale than a tool.

Legora aOS launched in May 2026 as the agentic operating system for legal work, with Legora Agent as its execution engine and seven layers underneath, from the models through the agentic harness, data and integrations, context and knowledge, legal capabilities, products and interfaces, and security and governance. Declaring the end of task-level legal AI is a category play. It also changes what the commercial motion has to look like.

What an OS sale actually is

You cannot sell an operating system into one practice group. It is firm-wide, multi-year, displaces the point tools already in the building, carries real switching cost, and needs a named executive sponsor inside the firm to survive the committee. That is the enterprise platform motion, and it is the one I have run for a decade.

Adoption is the bottleneck, not capability

The honest risk on an agentic platform is not whether it works. It is whether lawyers hand agents substantive work rather than dabble. Legora already answers this structurally by embedding Legal Engineers and driving adoption practice area by practice area. A revenue leader’s job is to make that land: the contract is firm-wide, the adoption is earned one practice at a time.

Governance is a revenue layer

Security and governance sits as its own layer in the aOS, not as a footnote: ethical walls, cross-matter isolation, SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, GDPR, HIPAA. ISO 42001 in particular certifies the AI management system rather than general infosec. In a Canadian firm or bank, that layer is where the deal is actually decided.

Where my experience maps

I sold a stack with the same shape: a data and context foundation, the workflow layer above it, agents and governance across the top, and the interfaces people actually work in. I can tell you which layer a Snowflake, a Databricks, or a Microsoft workspace occupies instead, and what governance a firm keeps or loses on the swap. Fluency in the architecture, not a claim to have invented it.

First 90 days

What I would do before changing anything.

A playbook written in advance is a hypothesis. This is the sequence I would run to earn one, against a competitor that opened in Toronto six months earlier.

1 – 30

Learn the deal, not just the product

Ride every live cycle without taking one over. Sit with the Legal Engineers through demos, use case design, and pilots, because they hold the ground truth on why firms convert. Reconstruct the last several wins and losses against the incumbent competitor. Catalogue every objection raised in a security or privilege review, verbatim.

31 – 60

Fix qualification and the forecast

Build the qualification scorecard out of what the won deals actually had in common, not out of a framework. Map the firm-side buying committee properly: managing partner, knowledge and innovation lead, CIO, risk. Establish a forecast cadence I would defend to a board, and name the practice-area beachheads inside accounts already signed.

61 – 90

Build the expansion motion

Turn firm references into the second wave, since every firm-wide deployment is a warm path to the general counsel on the other side of the engagement. Set the coverage model against the concentrated set of logos that decide this market, hire against the gaps it exposes, and publish the playbook only once it has survived contact with real buyers.

Sellers do not close deals, buyers do.

How I lead

Obsessive facilitation, not obsessive control.

The coaching principle

Sellers do not close deals, buyers do. The rep’s job is to earn the project-manager seat inside the buyer’s own process, because most of the cycle happens in rooms we are not invited to. I coach to that, not to activity counts.

Discovery before demo

The fastest way to lose a regulated deal is to demo into a room you have not qualified. I hold the line on discovery quality even when the demo is the easier meeting to book.

Playbooks from live deals

A playbook written in advance is a hypothesis. I build it out of the cycles the team is actually running, then make it repeatable once it has survived contact with real buyers.

Methodology

Challenger, Sandler Silver, and JB Sales certified. JB Sales for prospecting and velocity, Sandler for commercial and enterprise discovery and multi-stakeholder complexity.

In the field

Selling, teaching, and building community.
